newsitem.title: USA: Council sets 1997 Alaskan pollock harvest caps.
newsitem.headline: Council sets 1997 Alaskan pollock harvest caps.

text.p: Federal officials have cut the allowable harvest for Bering Sea pollock, but made up part of the difference by boosting the much-smaller Gulf of Alaska pollock harvest by 45 percent, officials said on Saturday.
The North Pacific Fishery Management Council accepted scientific recommendations and set the 1997 Bering Sea catch at 1.13 million metric tons, a 5 percent decline from the 1996 cap.

After setting the Bering Sea harvest limits for pollock and other groundfish species late Friday, the council on Saturday voted to allow the commercial fishing industry a 79,890 metric ton pollock catch in the Gulf of Alaska in 1997, up from the 54,810 metric tons allowed this year.

Fishery managers cut the Bering Sea pollock harvest in response to conservation concerns. Scientists advising the council cited a drop in the Bering Sea biomass and a shift in age distribution of the fish.

Environmentalists recommended Bering Sea harvest cuts of 25 percent to 40 percent. They said they were disappointed, but not surprised, by the council's action to cut only 60,000 metric tons from the Bering Sea cap.

"I think that the concerns that we're raising are legitimate, and a lot of people are seeing that," said Fred Munson of Greenpeace, a group that has warned of interwoven ecological problems in the Bering Sea.
He said the commercial fishing industry had large investments that made harvest reductions difficult. "It's hard to ask people to do this," he said of the deep harvest cuts.
National Marine Fisheries Service scientists advising the panel defended the Bering Sea harvest cap as prudent, and Gulf of Alaska pollock stocks are healthy enough to stand the harvest boost.

The council, one of the regional panels that operates under the auspices of the U.S. Commerce Department, manages fisheries in U.S. waters off the Alaska coast. It was scheduled to end its monthly meeting in Anchorage on Sunday.

The Alaskan pollock catch is by far the largest fish harvest in the nation, accounting in past years for about 40 percent of the nation's commercially landed seafood. The whitefish is sold in fillets, in minced product and in surimi, a seafood paste used to make imitation shellfish.

In addition to setting pollock harvest limits, the council on Friday and Saturday also set harvest limits for other species, including Pacific cod, fished in federal waters of the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea.
